opus-5.5.text:
I think the range is actually much broader than people usually imagine, and that's part of why I find world models so exciting. Language models gave us a general interface to knowledge and reasoning in text. A world model is about something more fundamental: understanding how the physical and visual world works, how things move, interact, persist, and change over time. Once you have a reasonably good general-purpose model of that, many verticals become natural downstream applications rather than separate research problems.

The most obvious one is **robotics and embodied AI**. A robot needs to predict what happens when it pushes, grasps, or navigates. Today we collect huge amounts of task-specific data for that. With a strong world model, you could simulate, plan, and imagine outcomes before acting. That changes the data economics of robotics completely.

Then there's **autonomous driving**, which has really been an early world-model domain all along. You're predicting other agents, rare events, long-tail scenarios. A general model could generate and reason about corner cases you'd never collect enough real data for.

**Content creation** is the more visible one right now: video generation, games, interactive environments, film previs. But I'd caution that generating pretty pixels isn't the same as having a world model. The real test is consistency, controllability, and whether the model respects physics and causality over long horizons. Entertainment may be where the money shows up first, but it shouldn't define the research goal.

Beyond that, there are less flashy but very important areas: **scientific simulation**, such as materials, fluids, and biology, where learned models can complement or accelerate traditional solvers. There's **AR and spatial computing**, where you need to understand 3D space and people's intentions in real time. And there's **digital twins** for manufacturing, logistics, and urban planning.

My view is that we shouldn't build a separate world model for each vertical from scratch. The more promising path is a strong foundation that learns visual and spatial representations, ideally grounded in perception rather than just pixel prediction, and then adapts to domains with relatively little additional data. That's the same lesson we learned from language and from representation learning in vision: generality pays off.

Honestly, we're still early. The definition of "world model" itself is still fuzzy in the community. But I think in a few years we'll look back and see that many of these verticals were limited by the absence of a good general model of the world, not by anything specific to their own domain.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as a source of comparison, saying they gave us an interface to knowledge and reasoning in text. It does not present language models as a vertical built on a general-purpose world model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, and that's actually what makes it exciting. But let me give you the way I think about it.

If a world model really learns something close to how the physical world works—how objects move, how light behaves, how things persist and interact over time—then it becomes a kind of substrate. It's not the product; it's the thing many products get built on top of. That's the analogy to language models. Nobody built GPT because they wanted to write emails. The emails, the coding assistants, the customer service tools all came after, once the general capability existed.

So the verticals I see most clearly, roughly in order of how soon I think they're real:

The first is content creation, broadly. Video generation, game asset generation, film pre-visualization. This is already happening, and it's the lowest-hanging fruit because the output is the pixels themselves. If the model generates something that looks right, you're done. You don't need the internal representation to be physically correct, you just need it to be convincing.

The second is simulation for robotics and embodied agents. This is the one I personally care most about. Right now, the bottleneck in robotics isn't really the policy learning—it's data. You can't collect ten million hours of real-world robot interaction. But if a world model can serve as a learned simulator, you can train and evaluate agents inside it. The catch here is that "looks right" is no longer enough. The dynamics have to actually be right, or the agent learns the wrong thing. That's a much harder bar, and I think people underestimate the gap between generating a beautiful video and generating a physically faithful one.

Third is autonomous driving, which is sort of a special case of the second. Companies are already using generative models to synthesize rare scenarios—the edge cases you can't collect enough of in the real world. That's a very concrete, very valuable vertical.

Then there's a longer tail: scientific simulation, like fluid dynamics or molecular behavior, where you'd want the model to have internalized real physics. Architecture and design, where you want to walk through a space before it exists. Education. Even things like sports analytics, predicting how a play unfolds.

But I want to push back a little on the framing of "vertical domains built on a general model," because I'm not certain the general model is the end state. There's a real tension. A truly general world model needs to cover an enormous distribution, and there's a question of whether you get sharper, more reliable behavior in a specific domain by fine-tuning a general model or by training something more targeted. In language, the general model won decisively. In vision and video, I think the jury is still out, because the modality is so much higher-dimensional and the failure modes are much less forgiving. A hallucinated word is annoying. A hallucinated physical interaction in a robot simulator can be dangerous.

So my view is: yes, the range of verticals is enormous, probably larger than what we saw with language, because the physical world touches everything. But the order in which they become real will be dictated by how much each one tolerates imperfection. Entertainment first, because it tolerates a lot. Robotics and science later, because they tolerate very little. And the research question that determines how fast we move down that list is whether we can make these models actually understand the world, rather than just render it.

r001.rationale: The response uses language models as an analogy for products built on a general capability, but does not frame language models themselves as a vertical built on a general-purpose world model.

astra-6.text:
I think the range could be quite broad. If you have a world model that captures how an environment evolves and how actions affect it, that becomes a foundation for many different tasks. Robotics is an obvious example, but you can also imagine applications in autonomous driving, games, or tools for designing and testing things in simulation.

The interesting question is what you share across those domains and what still needs to be specialized. A general-purpose model might provide useful knowledge about objects, space, and interactions. But each application has its own actions, constraints, and requirements for accuracy. A model that produces a plausible scene isn’t necessarily reliable enough to control a robot.

So I would think of it as a shared foundation with specialized systems built around it. The opportunity is to avoid learning everything from scratch for each vertical. How far that shared foundation can take us is still an open question.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics, autonomous driving, games, and simulation as possible applications, but it does not identify language models as a vertical built on the world model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the range could be very broad. If a general-purpose world model can learn how environments evolve and how actions change them, then that foundation could support robotics, autonomous driving, games, and tools for creating or simulating environments. These applications look different, but they share a need to understand dynamics and predict what might happen next.

The key question is what you still need to build for each domain. A robot needs an action interface and feedback from the physical world. A creative tool needs ways for people to control the output. So a general world model wouldn’t automatically become every product. It could provide a shared foundation, while domain-specific data, interfaces, and evaluation turn that foundation into something useful.

I’d also be careful about equating a convincing video with a reliable world model. For entertainment, something that looks plausible may be enough. For a robot interacting with people, you need much stronger evidence that its predictions are accurate. That difference will shape which vertical applications become practical first.

r001.rationale: The response names robotics, autonomous driving, games, and creative or simulation tools as possible applications, but it does not frame language models as a vertical built on a general-purpose world model.
